title: The way we used to work

fn.en: Talk about finished habits and past situations.

gr: used to and would for finished habits

can.en: I can describe how things used to be and what people would do in those days.

useful: Things aren’t like they used to be

acts.say: Say which column your parents’ working life belongs in.

items.s: She ___ her job on the Friday and started the new one on the Monday.

items.q: His company has a good ___ for looking after its staff.
The ___ of the work matters more to her than the salary.

It is her most ___ possession — her mother gave it to her.

sub.en: A finished habit, or a finished state? They do not take the same forms.

items.q: My grandfather ___ for the same railway for forty years.
items.why: used to + infinitive describes a finished habit or a long past situation.

items.q: Every morning he ___ walk to the depot, whatever the weather.
items.why: would also describes a repeated past action — but only an action, never a state.

items.q: There ___ a canteen in every branch.
items.why: be is a state, so would is not possible here. Only used to works.

items.q: She ___ three languages when she was younger.
items.why: know, speak, have, be and other state verbs take used to, not would.

items.q: ___ you use to work at the Karaganda branch?
items.why: The question is formed with did + use to (no d).

items.q: I ___ to enjoy Mondays, but I do now.
In those days everybody ___ home at six, and that was that.
She ___ getting up at five now — it doesn’t bother her at all.
items.why: be used to + -ing means “accustomed to”. It is a different structure from used to + infinitive.

rows: He used to work on the railway.
Every morning he would walk to the depot.
There used to be a canteen in every branch.
I didn’t use to enjoy Mondays.
Did you use to work there?
She is used to getting up at five.

lines: My grandfather [used to work|would work once|was used to work] for the same railway for forty years.
Every morning he [would|used|did use to be] walk to the depot, whatever the weather.
There [used to be|would be|would have been] a canteen in every branch.
[Did|Do|Were] you use to work at the Karaganda branch?
I [didn’t use|didn’t used|wasn’t used] to enjoy Mondays, but now I do.

items.why: After did, the form is use to, without the d.
be is a state, and would does not work with states.
be used to + -ing means accustomed to; a finished habit takes used to + infinitive.

acts.title: The way we used to work
text: My grandfather worked for the same railway for forty-one years. He started at sixteen, in a job his own father had found for him, and he retired from the office two floors above the one where he began. That was not unusual. In those days a working lifetime and an employer were more or less the same thing.

The working conditions would horrify anybody under thirty now. There used to be a rule about the length of your break, another about who could use which entrance, and a procedure for almost everything. He would arrive at ten to seven every morning and walk the last kilometre, because the bus did not go that way. Nobody ever asked whether he enjoyed it.

But there were things we have quietly lost. Every branch used to have a canteen, and the whole depot would stop and eat together at half past twelve. The company paid for a summer festival that everybody’s children went to. Accommodation for younger workers was rent-free. When my grandfather was ill for three months, nobody suggested that his job might not be there afterwards.

In recent years the pattern seems to be changing again, in a direction nobody expected. Thousands of young Europeans, who used to look north and west for work, now move to Africa, Asia and South America instead. They quit good jobs for temporary contracts abroad, and most of them say the same two things: the conditions are better and the work is more relaxed.

My grandfather would not have understood any of it. He valued one thing above all others, and it was the thing his employer gave him for forty-one years without ever being asked: a reason to expect that next year would look like this one.

items.s: The writer’s grandfather changed employer several times.
There used to be a rule about which entrance people could use.
The company provided rent-free accommodation for younger workers.
The writer says nothing good has been lost.
Young Europeans are now taking jobs in Africa, Asia and South America.
According to the writer, the grandfather valued the money most of all.

items.q: the whole of a person’s life (noun)
the official way something must be done (noun)

tts: For many years people moved to Europe in search of a brighter future and a higher standard of living. In recent years, however, the pattern seems to be changing.
Dermot came to the Philippines in 2005 for a job in property. At that time Ireland was doing well, and a lot of people couldn’t understand why he was going abroad.
It was a fantastic opportunity: he was quickly promoted to manager, when he had just been a sales person back in Ireland. The job also came with rent-free accommodation.
Maria is a qualified architect, but when she was made redundant in Athens she couldn’t find another job. She used to spend all day ringing people up and getting nowhere.
She still hasn’t been able to find work as an architect in Melbourne, but she has been able to retrain as a landscape designer.
Joaquim’s job in Luanda is temporary, for four months, but now he is there he thinks he will stay much longer. The working conditions are much better than in Lisbon.

items.q: What did Dermot’s job in the Philippines come with?
What did Maria use to do all day in Athens?
o: Ring people up and get nowhere

items.q: Why does Joaquim want to stay in Luanda?
o: The working conditions are much better than at home

write.q: Write about how work or study used to be for you, or for somebody in your family. Use used to for the situations and states, would for the actions that were repeated, and at least one didn’t use to.
write.ph: Ten years ago I used to…
plan: what the situation used to be
what you would do every day
what you didn’t use to do
write.model: Ten years ago I used to work in a shop on Prospekt Bukhar Zhyrau, six days a week. There used to be four of us on a shift; now the same shop runs with two and a self-service till. Every morning we would open at half past eight, and every morning the same three men would be waiting outside for their newspapers. I didn’t use to mind the hours. What I couldn’t stand was the last hour, when nobody came in and the clock stopped moving. Things aren’t like they used to be, and honestly I am glad. But I still miss those three men.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute about how something used to be — your school, your first job, your street. Use used to and would, and finish by saying what has changed.
speak.model: I used to work in a shop on Bukhar Zhyrau. There used to be four of us on a shift; now there are two and a machine. Every morning we would open at half eight, and the same three men would be waiting outside for their papers. I didn’t use to mind the hours. Things aren’t like they used to be — but I still think about those three men.
